name: Kripapureeswarar Temple, Tiruvennainallur
deity: Shiva as Kripapureeswarar (Arutkondanathar), with the goddess Mangalambigai
period: Ancient Shaiva shrine sung in the Tevaram (8th century); present structure of the Chola period with later additions
summary: Tiruvennainallur is the shrine where, tradition holds, Shiva stopped the saint Sundarar's wedding to claim him as his own and here received his first Tevaram hymn — the temple of Arutkondanathar, the Lord who takes his devotees by grace.

sections.history: Tiruvennainallur stands in the old Nadu Nadu country, between the Chola and Thondai lands, and has been a place of Shaiva pilgrimage since the age of the Nayanar saints, who sang of it in the Tevaram and made it a Paadal Petra Sthalam. Its fame is inseparable from the saint Sundarar, for it was here that his life as a poet of god began. The present stone temple is held to be the work of the Cholas, with a renovation remembered in the reign of Uttama Chola in the late tenth century, and it has been kept in worship through the centuries since. The town's name, read as the town of butter, carries its own old story of the goddess's devotion.
sections.architecture: The temple is a Dravidian complex entered from the east, its sanctum holding the linga of Kripapureeswarar, with the goddess Mangalambigai in her own shrine. The most revered object in the temple is a pair of padukas, the sacred footwear that the Lord is said to have left behind when he vanished here, and these are honoured in their own place. Mandapas and corridors in the Chola manner surround the sanctum, and the temple tank and the shrine of Sundarar keep the memory of the saint close to the heart of the worship.
sections.legends: The great legend of Tiruvennainallur is the taking of Sundarar. On the saint's wedding day, as Nambi Arooran prepared to marry, an old brahmin broke into the ceremony and claimed the bridegroom as his hereditary bondsman, showing a palm-leaf deed to prove it. The matter was carried to the village assembly here at Tiruvennainallur, where the deed was read and found true; and the old man, revealing himself as Shiva, led Sundarar to this temple and vanished near the sanctum, leaving only his footwear behind. Taken thus by grace, Sundarar broke into song, and his first words — calling the Lord the madman who wears the crescent moon — became the opening of his Tevaram. From this the Lord is praised as Arutkondanathar, he who stopped the wedding and claimed the devotee as his own.
sections.festivals: The festival dearest to the temple is the Aadi Swathi in July or August, a two-day celebration of Sundarar on his star. The ten-day Panguni Uthiram in March or April, with its flag-hoisting and float festival, is the great annual event, and the Margazhi Tiruvadhirai in December or January, the Aavani butter-offering, and Skanda Sashti are all kept with devotion. Maha Shivaratri and the monthly Pradosham are observed as at every Shiva temple. Dates follow the Tamil calendar, so confirm them locally.
sections.experience: Come to Tiruvennainallur for the nearness of a story, not for grandeur. Enter from the east to the sanctum of Kripapureeswarar, pause before the goddess Mangalambigai, and seek out the padukas that the devout believe the Lord left when he claimed Sundarar here. Many who visit carry in mind the image of the saint, stopped on his wedding day and led to god, and the temple rewards those who come to stand quietly where that turning is remembered. The town is unhurried, and an early morning or a lamplit evening suits it best.

visit.timings: Typically open in the morning and again from late afternoon into the evening, with a midday break; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the entrance stands.
visit.photography: Photography is generally permitted in the outer corridors and courtyards but prohibited inside the inner sanctum, in keeping with Tamil Nadu temple rules. Ask temple staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Tiruvennainallur lies in Villupuram district, reached by road from Villupuram and Tirukkovilur; Villupuram is the nearest major railway junction, and Puducherry and Tiruchirappalli are the nearest airports. Buses serve the town, and the temple stands at its centre.
